title: The Perception of Visual Surfaces
research_question: To test the hypothesis that the impression of the slant of a visual surface is determined by the rate of change (gradient) of texture-density in the retinal image, in isolation from other depth cues.

participants.description: 10 paid Os (9 women: 3 students, 3 clerical workers, 3 psychology teachers; 1 man: engineer) for the main experiment. An additional 32 different Os for a substantiation experiment.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Lantern slides of wallpaper patterns (regular rectangular elements and irregular unfamiliar elements) photographed at physical slants of 10°, 22°, 30°, and 45° from the perpendicular. These slides were projected onto a translucent screen, creating retinal images with varying gradients of texture-density (upward or downward density increase).

measures.instrument: A 6-inch square composition-board, adjustable by O's right hand, rotated 90° backward or forward from a vertical plane. O adjusted the board until the tactual-kinesthetic impression matched the visual impression of slant.

findings.antecedent: Retinal gradient of texture-density (corresponding to physical slants of 10°, 22°, 30°, 45°)
findings.mechanism: The retinal gradient of texture-density, in isolation from other factors, determines apparent optical slant.
findings.quote: The positive slopes of the lines joining the means actually obtained show that an increase in 'equivalent physical slant' is accompanied by an increase in the judged slant.

findings.consequent: Differential sensitivity to slant (as indicated by amount of increase in apparent slant for successive gradients and standard deviations)
findings.mechanism: Regular texture yields a more definite impression of slant, possibly by affording a more definite gradient of density than irregular texture.
findings.quote: Apparently the regular texture yields a more definite impression of slant.

findings.antecedent: Upward density increase of regular texture (physical slant equivalent to gradient: 10°, 22°, 30°, 45°)
findings.consequent: Judged backward slant (mean values: 0.8° fwd, 8.6° bkd, 18.9° bkd, 25.3° bkd)

findings.antecedent: Downward density increase of regular texture (physical slant equivalent to gradient: 10°, 22°, 30°, 45°)
findings.consequent: Judged forward slant (mean values: 8.5° fwd, 15.9° fwd, 21.9° fwd, 28.6° fwd)

findings.antecedent: Upward density increase of irregular texture (physical slant equivalent to gradient: 10°, 22°, 30°, 45°)
findings.consequent: Judged backward slant (mean values: 6.4° bkd, 7.8° bkd, 9.9° bkd, 23.9° bkd)

findings.antecedent: Downward density increase of irregular texture (physical slant equivalent to gradient: 10°, 22°, 30°, 45°)
findings.consequent: Judged forward slant (mean values: 8.6° fwd, 7.7° fwd, 9.2° fwd, 17.9° fwd)

findings.antecedent: Experimental setup (visibility of projection screen texture, absence of differential blur, absence of accommodation cue, hole-screen slant, residual head-motion)
findings.consequent: Judged slants consistently biased towards a frontal surface (compromise between slanted and frontal impression)
findings.mechanism: Conflicting cues (e.g., screen texture, lack of blur) favored a frontal perception, leading to a compromise in judged slant.
findings.quote: The discrepancy between the judged slant and the 'physical slant equivalent to the gradient' is consistently in the direction of a frontal surface.

findings.consequent: Greater individual differences in judged slant
findings.mechanism: Irregular texture functions less efficiently to determine slant, leading to more variability in perception among individuals.
findings.quote: There were notably greater individual differences in the case of the irregular texture, and this is additional evidence that an irregular texture functions less efficiently to determine slant.

findings.antecedent: Increase in gradient of density of texture (in a single-judgment, between-subjects design)
findings.consequent: Increase in amount of judged slant
findings.mechanism: Psychophysical correspondence between texture gradient and perceived slant is obtained even without opportunity for inferential improvement.
findings.quote: As in the main experiment, an increase in the gradient is accompanied by an increase in amount of judged slant, though the curves have less slope.

findings.antecedent: Differences in experimental setup (more visible projection screen texture, second hole-screen farther from O, adjustable board always pre-set at objective vertical)
findings.consequent: Lesser slopes in the curves (less steep increase in judged slant for increasing gradient) in the substantiation experiment compared to the main experiment
findings.quote: There is evidence that the lesser slopes in this experiment are attributable to differences between the two set-ups.

mechanisms: The impression of slant of a surface at the point fixated depends on the rate of change of the density of texture at the fovea, as physical surfaces not perpendicular to the line of sight project texture-elements that get denser as the surface recedes.
Regular texture may afford a more definite gradient of density than irregular texture, leading to clearer impressions of slant.
The perspective of texture, as distinguished from the perspective of rectilinear outlines, is a fundamental basis for the impression of a three-dimensional environment.
moderators: Direction of density increase (upward vs. downward)
Experimental setup (e.g., visibility of screen texture, presence of differential blur, hole-screen distance, pre-setting of adjustable board)
implementation_implications: Controlling texture gradients in built environments could influence perceived depth and spatial qualities, as texture perspective is a fundamental basis for the impression of a three-dimensional environment.

The findings suggest a general approach for designing environments to elicit specific spatial perceptions by identifying and manipulating correlates in retinal stimulation for properties of the phenomenal environment.

tables.description: Means of judgments and medians of their standard deviations for judged slant as a function of the gradient of texture density (physical slant equivalent) for regular and irregular textures, with upward and downward density increases.

limitations: The texture of the translucent projection-screen itself had a contradictory gradient to the projected image, potentially affecting results.
The absence of differential blur in the projected image (all parts equally in focus) contradicted the texture-density gradient, favoring the perception of a frontal surface.
The experimental setup (e.g., hole-screens, headrest) eliminated motion parallax and binocular disparity, which are real-world depth cues.

Judged slants were consistently biased towards a frontal surface, indicating a compromise between the slanted impression and other cues favoring a frontal plane (e.g., hole-screen slant, residual head-motion).
The baseline for tactual-kinesthetic reproduction (objective vertical) had a constant error relative to the O's perceived vertical, requiring correction.
Some observers reported using inferential cues (size of elements, density, linear perspective) rather than immediate impressions, raising questions about the nature of the perception.
